summary: Specifies the Aggregate Server Access Protocol, which together with ENRP provides a high-availability data transfer mechanism over IP. It uses handle-based addressing, which separates a logical endpoint from its IP addresses, so clients can reach a pool of servers by name. It is an experimental protocol.

eli5.summary: Instead of knowing one shop's address, you ask for any shop in the group by name. This protocol lets clients do that, and move to another server if one stops answering.

subtitle: A protocol for client-facing access to server pools with handle-based load balancing and failover.

tldr.problem: Applications that need high availability must bind to specific server IP addresses, creating a single point of failure. When a server fails, clients must be manually redirected.
tldr.mechanism: ASAP uses logical pool handles instead of IP addresses. Clients ask a registry (ENRP) to resolve a pool handle to a list of available servers and can transparently fail over to another server in the pool if one becomes unreachable.
tldr.outcome: A client can reach a pool of servers by a single name, servers can be added or removed without client reconfiguration, and automatic failover reduces downtime.

today: RFC 5352 remains experimental and has not achieved widespread deployment in production systems. The ASAP/ENRP protocols are used in research environments and specialized applications that require high-availability server pooling.

sections.title: Pool Handles and Handle-Based Addressing
sections.content:
ASAP (Aggregate Server Access Protocol) provides a high-availability mechanism over IP by introducing pool handles: logical names for collections of servers. Instead of a client connecting to a single server at a specific IP address, it connects to a pool by name. The system then selects which server in the pool actually receives the traffic.

A pool handle is a logical pointer that isolates the communication endpoint from its physical addresses. This separation allows servers to be added, removed, or readdressed without changing what clients ask for. ASAP works with ENRP (Endpoint Handlespace Redundancy Protocol) to provide a fault-tolerant registry that maintains current pool membership.
sections.eli5: A pool handle is like asking for "any pizza shop in town" instead of "the pizza shop at 123 Main Street". The system picks which shop you go to, and if it closes, it sends you somewhere else.

sections.title: ASAP Message Types and Protocol Operations
sections.content:
ASAP defines 14 message types for communication between clients (pool users, PUs), servers (pool elements, PEs), and the registry (ENRP servers). The core messages are:

Registration: A PE sends ASAP_REGISTRATION to its home ENRP server to join or create a pool. The ENRP server responds with ASAP_REGISTRATION_RESPONSE, granting or denying the registration.

Handle Resolution: A client sends ASAP_HANDLE_RESOLUTION to ask the ENRP server which PEs belong to a pool. The response (ASAP_HANDLE_RESOLUTION_RESPONSE) includes a list of available pool element addresses. Clients can request automatic updates if the pool changes.

Keep-Alive and Error Reporting: An ENRP server periodically sends ASAP_ENDPOINT_KEEP_ALIVE to verify PEs are reachable. A PU or PE can report an unreachable endpoint with ASAP_ENDPOINT_UNREACHABLE. Cookies and business cards allow PEs to pass failover hints to clients.
sections.eli5: Servers tell the registry "I am in the pizza shop pool". Clients ask the registry "which pizza shops are available?". If something breaks, clients and servers tell the registry.

sections.title: Registration, Resolution, and Failover Procedures
sections.content:
When a PE starts, it must first find its home ENRP server (the ENRP_HUNT procedure). Once connected, it registers with ASAP_REGISTRATION, providing the pool handle and its transport addresses. The PE binds its SCTP association to all IP addresses it will use.

A client wanting to send to a pool sends ASAP_HANDLE_RESOLUTION. The home ENRP server returns a list of pool elements with their addresses and a load-sharing policy (commonly round-robin). ASAP can select a PE locally based on the policy or ask ENRP to choose.

When a PE becomes unreachable, ASAP can automatically try the next PE in the pool without notifying the client—transparent failover. ASAP uses timers and thresholds to detect unresponsive peers. A PE can send a COOKIE to a PU during normal operation; if the PE fails, the PU sends the cookie to a new PE to help restore state. A BUSINESS_CARD conveys the pool handle and preferred failover ordering.
sections.eli5: Servers register when they start up. Clients ask for the server list. If a server stops responding, clients try another one without missing a beat.

sections.title: Load Distribution Policies and Pool Dynamics
sections.content:
ASAP defines load-sharing policies for selecting which PE in a pool receives the next message. The basic policy is round-robin: clients cycle through available PEs in order. Other policies may be defined by implementations.

The ASAP interface lets applications request caching of pool information locally to reduce queries to the ENRP server. An application can request a specific PE handle (an address within a pool), a random PE from the pool, or even send directly to a transport address for direct peering.

Pools are dynamic. Members can be added or removed at any time without service interruption. If a client requests dynamic updates (the 'S' bit in ASAP_HANDLE_RESOLUTION), the ENRP server pushes new ASAP_HANDLE_RESOLUTION_RESPONSE messages whenever the pool membership changes. The client updates its local cache and begins routing to the new set.
sections.eli5: The system can split traffic evenly across servers or use custom rules. The list of available servers is kept fresh; if servers join or leave, clients learn about it.

sections.title: SCTP Transport and Multi-Homing
sections.content:
ASAP is designed to integrate deeply with SCTP (Stream Control Transmission Protocol), which provides multi-homing and redundancy at the transport layer. SCTP associations can use multiple IP addresses per endpoint, providing additional fault tolerance.

All ASAP messages between PEs and ENRP servers MUST use SCTP. Messages between PUs and ENRP servers MAY use SCTP or TCP. Data traffic between PEs and PUs MAY use any transport protocol registered by the PE.

A PE registering to a pool must bind its SCTP endpoint to all IP addresses it will advertise, ensuring the addresses used for ASAP communication are consistent with those advertised to the ENRP server.
sections.eli5: The system talks to registries using a reliable protocol (SCTP). Client-server data traffic can use anything, but the control messages between servers and the registry are SCTP-protected.

sections.title: Security Threats and Mitigation
sections.content:
ASAP deployments face threats including spoofing (attackers claiming to be legitimate PEs or ENRP servers), eavesdropping on pool membership information, and manipulation of pool contents by attackers.

The RFC recommends a chain of trust established at deployment time. ASAP endpoints can use IPsec to authenticate and encrypt all ASAP messages, or SCTP's optional HMAC-based authentication. Configuration of trust anchors, signing of ASAP messages, and validation of peer credentials are essential for secure deployments. Transport-level security (TLS or SCTP AUTH) can protect against eavesdropping and tampering.
sections.eli5: Bad actors could lie about which servers are available. The system should authenticate all registration and lookup messages to prevent this.
